node.label: Joy Parr
node.date_label: Labouring Children 1980 · 'Nature and Hierarchy' 1985 · The Gender of Breadwinners 1990 · 'Gender History and Historical Practice' 1995 · Domestic Goods 1999 · Sensing Changes 2010
node.description: A Canadian historian of work, gender, childhood, consumption and the environment. In 1985 she wrote that what set women and children apart as historical subjects was not nature but 'proximity to power', and asked historians to 'allow as a possibility that gender/sex hierarchies and class hierarchies function simultaneously, each according to its own logic, often in conflict'. The Gender of Breadwinners (1990) tested this in two Ontario towns, Paris, a knitting-mill town where most wage earners were women, and Hanover, a furniture town where most were men; reviewers quote it rejecting 'an ahistorical hierarchy of oppressions' and treating 'class/gender, male/female, market/nonmarket, public/private' as pairs whose meanings 'are multiple and mutable'. In the Left History exchange of 1995–96 Iacovetta and Kealey called her 'a major figure in the field' of gender history, while Sangster criticised the tie her 1995 essay drew between gender history and 'the post-structuralist premise that identities were made in relationships'; the labour historian Craig Heron praised the book but found that it had 'suppressed the impact of class' in a 1949 strike. Labouring Children (1980) grew from her Yale thesis on British child immigrants; later books turned to postwar household goods (Domestic Goods, 1999) and to sensory histories of megaprojects and environmental change (Sensing Changes, 2010).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Joy Parr (1949–2024); PhD Yale 1977 ('The Home Children: British Juvenile Immigrants to Canada, 1868–1924'); Labouring Children: British Immigrant Apprentices to Canada, 1869–1924 (1980); Childhood and Family in Canadian History (ed., 1982); “Nature and Hierarchy: Reflections on Writing the History of Women and Children” (Atlantis, 1985); “Disaggregating the Sexual Division of Labour” (CSSH, 1988); The Gender of Breadwinners: Women, Men, and Change in Two Industrial Towns, 1880–1950 (1990); “Gender History and Historical Practice” (CHR, 1995; reprinted in Gender and History in Canada, ed. with Mark Rosenfeld, 1996); “Household Choices as Politics and Pleasure in 1950s Canada” (ILWCH, 1999); Domestic Goods: The Material, the Moral, and the Economic in the Postwar Years (1999). After 2000: “Smells Like?” (Environmental History, 2006); Sensing Changes: Technologies, Environments, and the Everyday, 1953–2003 (2010). Readings: Drystek (1980); Heron, Guildford, Scheinberg and Dennis (1991); Bertaux (1992); Benson (1993); the Left History exchange (Sangster 1995, 1996; Dubinsky and Marks 1996; Iacovetta and Kealey 1996); Brush (2000); Owram (2001); Jackson and Rumiel (2011). Further selected bibliography: “Notes for a More Sensuous History of Twentieth-Century Canada: The Timely, the Tacit, and the Material Body” (2001).
node.scope_note: Her own words are read in 'Nature and Hierarchy' (Atlantis, 1985, pp. 39–44, in full), the first-page extract of the 1988 CSSH article and the abstract of the 1999 ILWCH article. Her books are not read here: The Gender of Breadwinners, Domestic Goods and Sensing Changes are quoted only as their reviewers quote them, with the reviewers' page references, and the 1995 CHR essay only as Iacovetta and Kealey (1996) and Sangster (1996) quote it. In-period reviews read in full: Drystek (1980), Heron (CHR, 1991), Guildford (Atlantis, 1991), Scheinberg (Archivaria, 1991), Dennis (EcHR, 1991), Bertaux (JEH, 1992), Benson (JAH, 1993), Brush (EH.NET, 2000); later reception: Owram (BC Studies, 2001); the four Left History papers of 1995–96 are read in full. She is not presented as a founder: her 1985 essay places itself among 'a good many others' asking for the change, and the Canadian gender-history debate also turned on Pierson (1991) and Scott. The 1995 CHR essay appeared in an issue of historiographical essays, not in a CHR exchange; the exchange that took it up was in Left History. The environmental work dates from 2006–10 and is used only for the environment edge; a 2026 CHR forum on The Gender of Breadwinners is a later reading. Canonical-work review (2026-10-24): added titles and dates are selected bibliography, not a complete career or a new reading of the books. Original works, translations, edited collections and posthumous editions are distinguished; earlier argument and source-reading qualifications remain.

incident_edges.relationship: Gender and class as simultaneous hierarchies, and gender history as a practice in Canadian women's history (1985–96)
incident_edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words (Atlantis, 1985, read in full): women and children are not tied together as subjects by nature; 'What distinguishes feminine and preschooler from masculine and prime of life is not naturalness versus artificiality but proximity to power' (p. 39). She criticises the mid-1970s Canadian literature on reform for characterising 1880–1920 as 'an era of "maternal feminism"', seeing women's public actions 'definitionally as an extension of the private' (p. 41), and asks historians to 'stop shying away from the word "patriarchy"' and to 'allow as a possibility that gender/sex hierarchies and class hierarchies function simultaneously, each according to its own logic, often in conflict' (p. 44). She presents this as a change 'a good many others have already begun to suggest' (p. 39). The Gender of Breadwinners (1990), unread here, as reviewers quote it: Guildford (Atlantis, 1991, p. 140) says she rejects 'an ahistorical hierarchy of oppressions' (p. 8) and argues 'that class and gender are made and experienced simultaneously'; Bertaux (JEH, 1992, p. 241) quotes p. 9 on 'these galloping pairs—class/gender, male/female, market/nonmarket, public/private' whose meanings 'are multiple and mutable'. Reception in the Left History exchange (all read in full): Sangster calls the book 'One of the path breaking books on gender history' (1995, p. 120); Iacovetta and Kealey call her 'recognized as a leading practitioner of gender history' (1996, p. 222) and 'a major figure in the field', quoting her 1995 CHR essay (pp. 362–63) that 'gender history made masculinity and femininity commensurably problematical historically, while insisting that neither could be well understood without companion inquiries into the other hierarchies with which they were mutually intertwined' (p. 228); Dubinsky and Marks cite her for refraining 'from imposing one category - be it class or gender - on historical actors' (1996, p. 211). Criticism: Sangster (1996, p. 240 n. 2) characterises Parr's essay (its reprint in Gender and History in Canada, 1996, p. 11, unread here) as placing critics 'feminist and anti-feminist alike, in the same oppositional group' (Sangster's wording, not a quotation from Parr), notes that she had been reproached for not offering 'more criticism of historians such as Mariana Valverde and Joy Parr' (p. 240 n. 3), and, quoting Parr's line that the move to gender 'began from the post-structuralist premise that identities were made in relationships' (reprint p. 14), questions 'the prevailing assumption that gender history as the field, post-structuralism as the method, equals a superior, more broad-minded history' (pp. 244, 246). The 1995 essay itself is unread: its words here are quoted by Iacovetta and Kealey and by Sangster. Not a founding: the field's gender debate also runs through Pierson (1991) and Scott (edge_891). Later reading, labelled: a 2026 CHR 'great books' forum (abstract only) calls the book 'a path-breaking study that challenged established dichotomies in social theory'.

incident_edges.relationship: Gender in the making of class: a women's town and a men's town, Paris and Hanover, Ontario (1985–90)
incident_edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words (Atlantis, 1985): 'students of men's work and men's participation in labour organisations', with women's historians and historians of childhood, 'have reified the skill-unskill boundary' (p. 42); 'Skill, too, is a socially constructed category' (pp. 42–43). Of the Marxist analysis in Women at Work, Ontario, 1850–1930 (1975) she writes, quoting feminist critics (n. 20: Phillips and Taylor; Hartmann), that it 'explains why a hierarchy of labour is necessary within the waged labour force, but tells us nothing about why women end up at the bottom of this hierarchy' (p. 43). The Gender of Breadwinners (1990; unread here) compares Paris and Hanover, Ontario. Heron, a labour historian, reviewing it (CHR, 1991, read in full): 'the most exhilarating, challenging book to appear in modern Canadian social history in many years'; it 'integrates and surpasses' women's, labour, technological and economic history, and 'Parr gives the boot to neo-classical analysis, simplistic Marxism, and radical feminism' (p. 218). He quotes its introduction that 'the parts and proportions of the social landscape covered by class and gender alter' (p. 10) but finds that in the 1949 Paris strike 'she has suppressed the impact of class where it was undeniably a crucial force' (p. 220). From her own figures he suggests that 'the portrait of the "women's town" may be slightly misleading' (p. 219). He also finds that she downplays the wars and the state and 'seldom makes any reference to the considerable Canadian literature on work, class, gender, or small-town life' (pp. 220–21). He concludes that she 'has pushed us onto new terrain where gender is neither ignored nor is it given a monocausal explanatory force' (p. 221). Scheinberg (Archivaria, 1991) sees 'a more dynamic alternative to the old and stale studies that focused more on workers' industrial and organizational activities', while doubting conclusions drawn from 'the testimony of seven women' (p. 175). Dennis (EcHR, 1991) calls it 'an important contribution to the literature of labour history and locality studies' (p. 762). A contribution from inside the field's gender strand, alongside Sangster (1989) and Bradbury (1993). It does not claim that labour history lacked gender before 1990. edge_842 and edge_889 (cdn_women_gender → cdn_working_class) already carry the entry-level contribution and critique.

incident_edges.relationship: British child immigrants as labouring children (1977–80), and childhood as a history of power (1985)
incident_edges.evidence_note: In-period. Her Yale PhD (1977), 'The Home Children: British Juvenile Immigrants to Canada, 1868–1924', is recorded in the AHA Directory of History Dissertations (record 45612; adviser Robin Winks). Drystek's review of Labouring Children (Archivaria 11, 1980–81, read in full) names the thesis as the source of its sample of 997 Barnardo case histories (p. 241). He quotes the book's aims: a 'study of the life and work of child immigrants in Britain and Canada' (p. 13) that would 'reveal a darker side of evangelicalism, of turn-of-the-century childhood, and of Canadian rural life than the record has so far been allowed to express' (p. 12). His reading is critical: 'because of the authors' almost uniformly negative approach, the study is of limited value', the sample's statistical basis is unexplained, and 'the argument that a British child immigrant suffered a special burden is not convincing' (pp. 241–42). The book itself is unread here. Her own words (Atlantis, 1985) turn the subject into a question about power: she finds it troubling to treat women and children 'as part of one subject', admits to being 'part of a group who wrote, reviewed, lectured and squabbled this cluster into convention', and asks 'Is it nature which ties women and children together as subjects? Clearly not' (p. 39); the family 'is experienced by members of different generations in very different ways' (p. 44). She also edited Childhood and Family in Canadian History (1982; title-level, see edge_792). A contribution among the field's early works, not its origin: Sutherland's Children in English-Canadian Society (1976) precedes it.

incident_edges.relationship: Disaggregating the sexual division of labour: gender and class compared across workplaces, read beyond Canada (1988–93)
incident_edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words: the CSSH article of 1988 (first-page extract read, p. 511) observes that 'economists and feminist theorists have been interested in sexual divisions as general features of the economic or sex/gender system rather than as boundaries between tasks forged in defined contexts by particular clashes of interest', and that 'most analysts have dealt with gender division as a characteristic of the work force as a whole'. Reviews of The Gender of Breadwinners outside Canada (all read in full): Benson (JAH, 1993, p. 1630) writes that 'few historians have successfully integrated the discussion of these two fundamental relationships' and that 'Parr joins this small but growing group'. On p. 1631 Benson continues: 'Like others influenced by post-structuralist theory, she emphasizes the shifting and multivalent meanings often obscured by dualisms'; Parr 'gives gender and class coordinate roles in her analysis but downplays ethnicity'. Dennis (EcHR, 1991) finds that she 'goes far beyond previous accounts of connections between capitalism and patriarchy' (p. 761) but faults graphs that 'cavalierly use straight lines to connect a handful of isolated observations' (p. 762). Bertaux (JEH, 1992) wants 'a basic quantitative summary of work force data' (p. 240) but concludes that 'the topic of gender and work is not strictly a "women's issue"' (p. 241). The book itself is unread here. This records reception in international journals, not adoption. Optional: edge_840 (cdn_women_gender → gender) already links the Canadian field to the international entry.

incident_edges.relationship: Postwar Canadian consumption as a politics of nation, class and gender: domestic goods, designers and householders (1999)
incident_edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words: the abstract of 'Household Choices as Politics and Pleasure in 1950s Canada' (ILWCH 55, 1999, a special issue on class and consumption) reads 'How much consumption matters is a cultural difference, a shared national predicament, a politics grounded in the circumstances of class, and learned as a gendered responsibility', and asks 'When producers were not paramount in the regulation of consumption, to what priorities was commerce subsidiary?' Domestic Goods (1999) is unread here; as Brush quotes it (EH.NET, 2000, read in full), it is 'an archeology of the material, moral, and economic choices and constraints which formed Canadian commodity culture in the two decades after the Second World War' (p. 17). It asks 'How much can citizens talk back to manufacturers and the state about domestic goods?' (pp. 3–4). It sets itself against accounts that 'naturalize[d] these hortatory American norms as the intrinsic qualities of "consumer society"' (p. 11), and it places studies of material culture 'into unaccustomed company' (p. 3). Brush notes that Parr 'locates the history of consumption as a history primarily of women as consumers, in contrast to the male-dominated fields of design and manufacturing'. Criticism: Owram (BC Studies 129, 2001, read in full) finds the book's 'strength is in its parts rather than in some seamless thesis' (p. 103). He reads her as arguing that 'the assumption of consumer sovereignty is facile' (p. 104), and answers that 'Canadians, both men and women, preferred Fords to Volvos, and that is what they got' (p. 105). edge_843 (cdn_women_gender ↔ consumption, comparison) is title-level; this edge adds read evidence.

incident_edges.relationship: Embodied, sensory histories of megaprojects and environmental change in Canada, 1953–2003 (2006–10)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Dated 2006–2011; no claim here concerns her work before 2000. Sensing Changes: Technologies, Environments, and the Everyday, 1953–2003 (UBC Press, 2010) is unread here. As Jackson quotes it (Senses and Society 6:2, 2011, read in full), Parr seeks to move beyond 'representations . . . in language . . . , to open interpretive space in which to study the robust materiality of technologies, environments, and the everyday, to encounter them as directly and as fleshly as possible' (p. 9). Jackson describes chapters on the NATO base at Gagetown, nuclear power and heavy water on Lake Huron, the St Lawrence Seaway at Iroquois, the Columbia River reservoir and Walkerton's water, each read through a sense ('Smell and Risk', 'Taste and Expertise'). She adds that Parr counts proprioception, kinesthetics and proxemics among the senses (pp. 225–27). Jackson places the book in the UBC Press Nature/History/Culture series (p. 225). Rumiel (Left History 15:1, 2011, read in full) notes 'the people whose lives and senses of self had been transformed' by megaprojects (p. 189). She suggests that 'a comparative analysis of a related case in a Canadian Aboriginal or Inuit community' was a missed opportunity (p. 189). The environmental line begins earlier with 'Smells Like?: Sources of Uncertainty in the History of the Great Lakes Environment' (Environmental History 11:2, 2006; metadata only). A contribution: it records her later field, not influence on environmental history's formation.

incident_edges.relationship: Her two-town study (1990) and 1995 essay deconstructed skill and treated 'portraits of experience' as 'interpretations, reclamations of sensations', while keeping 'materialist conceptions of work and the economy' (as read by Sangster, 2000)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Both Parr texts are unread (the existing Parr entry records the 1995 essay as known only through Iacovetta–Kealey and Sangster). Sangster 2000, read in full: the 'polar worlds of men's and women's work in small town Ontario' show 'the positive results of talking gender' (p. 151, citing The Gender of Breadwinners); Parr grouped with Tillotson, Mercedes Steedman and Creese as having 'deconstructed the notion of skill' while 'materialist conceptions of work and the economy are still in evidence, unlike the more radical, anti-materialist claims for deconstruction offered up by international scholars like Joan Scott' (p. 157); from the 1995 essay (p. 364) the sentence that portraits of experience 'were interpretations, reclamations of sensations which first had been organized, then claimed as experience' (p. 159, as quoted by Sangster). Moderate: a named reader's account.

incident_edges.relationship: Parr explicitly connects her questions about gender and class categories to Scott’s work on the politics of gender categories, among other named interlocutors.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Parr’s own introduction to The Gender of Breadwinners, printed p.9, relates the questions posed by her two town studies to Scott and Denise Riley, alongside Mary Poovey and R.W.Connell. This supports a bounded methodological resource, not exclusive derivation or identical conclusions. Selected introduction only; the whole book and cited works were not newly read. Original 1990 publication and later reprints/digital preview remain distinct.
